stories.title: Big News for Babies: Every Child Gets $70,000!
stories.headline_kid: The Singapore government announced that every Singaporean child will now receive about $70,000 in support as they grow up — the same amount no matter if they are the first or the fifth child in the family.
summary: Every year, Singapore's Prime Minister gives a big speech called the National Day Rally, where he shares important plans for the country. This year, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a brand-new package to help parents raise their children.

Right now, families get different amounts of money depending on whether their child is the first, second or third born, under something called the Baby Bonus Scheme. The new plan changes this — every Singaporean child will get roughly the same total support, worth about $70,000, spread out over their growing years.

This money is not given as one big cheque. Instead, it comes through several ways: cash gifts when a baby is born, top-ups into a special savings account for the child, and other forms of financial help along the way, like for school and daily needs.

PM Wong said helping families is one of the most important things the government can do. By making support equal for every child, the government hopes more couples will feel encouraged to have children, and that raising kids will feel less costly for everyone.

lenses.me: If you have a younger brother or sister born after this new scheme starts, they might get support in a slightly different way than you did — but it will be fair either way.
lenses.family: Parents thinking of having more children may feel more confident, since every child gets similar support, not less for a third or fourth baby.
lenses.friends: Some of your classmates' families might talk about this at home, especially if they have younger siblings on the way.
lenses.nation: Singapore has one of the lowest birth rates in the world, so this plan aims to make having children feel more affordable and encourage more babies to be born.
lenses.world: Many countries, like Japan and South Korea, also worry about too few babies being born — so other nations may watch how well Singapore's plan works.

stories.title: More Families Can Now Apply for HDB Flats
stories.headline_kid: The government is raising the income limit for buying government flats, so more families can qualify — and parents with children now get an extra chance in the ballot.
summary: Most Singaporeans live in HDB flats, which are homes built and sold by the government at a lower price than private housing. To buy a new flat directly from HDB — called a Build-To-Order or 'BTO' flat — a family's monthly income must not go above a certain limit, called the income ceiling.

During the National Day Rally, PM Wong announced that this income ceiling will be raised for both BTO flats and Executive Condominiums (a slightly fancier type of government housing). This means families who earn a bit more money, and previously could not apply, will now be allowed to.
There is more good news for parents: families with children will get an extra ballot chance, like getting an extra lucky-draw ticket, which improves their odds of successfully getting a flat.
Because these changes affect how people plan their housing, the next BTO sale has been pushed back from October to November, giving families more time to review their options before applying.

lenses.me: If your family is planning to move house one day, these changes could make it a little easier for your parents to qualify for a new flat.
lenses.family: Parents who earn slightly more but still couldn't apply for a BTO flat before may now finally have a chance.
lenses.friends: Classmates whose parents are saving up for a new home might mention this change happening around their dinner table.
lenses.nation: Housing is one of the biggest costs for Singaporean families, so making flats more accessible helps more people afford a stable home.
lenses.world: Singapore's public housing system is often studied by other countries as a model for how governments can help citizens own affordable homes.

stories.title: Preschool Fees Are Getting Much Cheaper by 2030
stories.headline_kid: By 2030, parents will pay a lot less for childcare and infant care at government-supported preschools in Singapore.
summary: Before children start Primary 1, many attend preschool or childcare centres so their parents can go to work. But preschool fees can be expensive, especially for infant care, which looks after babies younger than 18 months.

In his National Day Rally speech, PM Wong announced that the government will pay for a bigger share of these costs. This means that by the year 2030, families sending their children to government-supported preschools will pay significantly lower fees than before.

PM Wong explained that helping with preschool costs is 'one of the best investments' the country can make, because good early education helps children learn important skills before they even start primary school.
This change is expected to make life easier for working parents, especially those juggling jobs and young children, and may also encourage more families to enrol their children in quality preschools.

lenses.me: If you have a younger sibling starting preschool soon, your parents might end up paying less for their childcare fees.
lenses.family: Parents can save money that used to go towards expensive childcare fees, which can be used for other family needs instead.
lenses.friends: Some of your friends' parents who run small businesses or work full-time may talk about how helpful this change is for their household budget.
lenses.nation: Lower preschool costs may encourage more parents to return to work, helping Singapore's economy while supporting families.
lenses.world: Many countries are trying to make early childhood education more affordable, so Singapore's move adds to this global trend.

stories.title: Singapore May Dig a Tunnel Under the Sea to Pulau Tekong
stories.headline_kid: Singapore is studying whether to build a tunnel deep under the sea to connect Pulau Tekong, where army recruits train, to the mainland — and Sentosa may get exciting new attractions too.
summary: Pulau Tekong is an island north-east of mainland Singapore, best known as the place where young men do their Basic Military Training when they join National Service. Right now, people can only reach it by boat.

During the National Day Rally, plans were revealed to study building an undersea tunnel — like a road that runs beneath the seabed instead of over a bridge — to connect Tekong to the mainland. This could make travelling to and from the island faster and easier in future.

Sentosa, Singapore's popular island for beaches and theme parks, and its smaller neighbour Pulau Brani are also set for a makeover. There are plans for new attractions and better connections linking these islands to each other and to the mainland.
These are still early studies, which means nothing has been built yet, but they show how Singapore keeps thinking of creative ways to use its limited land and sea space wisely.

lenses.me: If you ever visit Sentosa or have a family member doing National Service on Tekong, these changes could shape how you travel there one day.
lenses.family: Families who enjoy day trips to Sentosa might get to enjoy new attractions and smoother travel between the islands in future.
lenses.friends: Older brothers, cousins or family friends who will serve National Service might one day travel to Tekong through a tunnel instead of a ferry.
lenses.nation: Since Singapore is a small country, building underground and undersea helps create more usable space without needing more land.
lenses.world: Countries like Japan and Norway have also built long undersea tunnels, so Singapore can learn from their engineering experience.

stories.title: Three Southern Islands Could Become One Giant New Island
stories.headline_kid: Singapore is planning to join three southern islands — Semakau, Bukom and Pulau Sudong — into one big new island for future factories and power needs.
summary: South of mainland Singapore lie several small islands. Semakau is where Singapore's rubbish is safely buried after burning, Bukom is home to an oil refinery, and Pulau Sudong is a smaller island nearby.

During the National Day Rally, plans were announced to merge these three islands into a single, larger island using land reclamation, which is when sand and materials are added to the sea to create new land — similar to how Jurong Island, home to many chemical and oil companies, was created by joining several small islands together.
This new island could be used to house advanced factories and future power infrastructure, meaning things like power plants that generate electricity for Singapore's homes and businesses.
Since Singapore is a small country with little land, combining islands like this allows the country to plan ahead for future industries without taking up space needed for homes, schools, or parks.

lenses.me: You might not visit these islands yourself, but the electricity and products made there could one day power the lights and gadgets in your own home.
lenses.family: Your family's home may one day get electricity generated from power infrastructure built on this new merged island.
lenses.friends: Classmates who are interested in geography or engineering might find it fascinating how islands can be joined together like puzzle pieces.
lenses.nation: This project shows how Singapore carefully plans its limited land to balance industry, energy needs and environmental care for the future.
lenses.world: Land reclamation projects like this are watched closely by other small, land-scarce countries looking for similar solutions.
